page_title: Moving from orchestration to choreography - Part 2

sources.entry: Moving from orchestration to choreography - By Olivier Jauze, March 2021. Michelin's journey from BPM orchestration to event-driven choreography. It's the first of a series and continues with part 2 and part 3.

summary.title: Moving from orchestration to choreography - Part 2
summary.one_liner: Learn how Michelin assembled a remote team during COVID lockdown and built a Kafka Streams and microservices choreography to replace a central BPM orchestrator.
keywords: how to migrate from bpm to microservices
takeaways: Event storming helps describe business processes as business events, and the team must avoid an orchestrator-centric view when doing so.
Remote architecture and product workshops can be run with Teams and Miro, but they are tiring and need limits on daily duration and time for team bonding.
Kafka Connect, Kafka Streams microservices and a central Kafka broker formed the target architecture; Kafka ran on-premise on VMware while microservices ran in Azure Kubernetes.
Monitoring combined Prometheus and Grafana on JMX metrics for technical health, with Splunk dashboards for functional support views.
Frequent production deployments (25 in about 15 months, one rollback) and automated Gitlab CI pipelines were central to the approach.
summary.summary: This is Part 2 of a Michelin series on moving from a central BPM orchestrator (DOO) to an event-driven choreography of microservices. It covers the scale of the legacy system, how a hybrid team was assembled and run remotely during the first COVID-19 lockdown using the Scoping 360 method, and an event storming session that surfaced language and bounded-context issues. It then describes the technical architecture (Kafka, Kafka Connect, Kafka Streams in Java, Gitlab CI, Prometheus/Grafana, Splunk) and reports on production results and a resilience incident. The article is an experience report with no code, and it says Part 3 will go deeper into the technical solution.
